title: The Seahorse Lookalike That Is Not a Seahorse at All
summary: At first glance, this thumb-sized fish looks like a seahorse. It has a horse-shaped head tilted down, a curled tail, and a pouch for the young in males. But scientists say it is not a seahorse. In a new study in the Journal of Lost Species, they describe Australyichthys aegis, from deep reefs off southern Australia. They call it the helmethead sea muppet for its helmet-like crest. With the bullneck sea muppet and the paradoxical sea muppet, it forms a new group, Australyichthys. Only seven are known, found over about 65 years along more than 2,500 kilometers of coast. None has been collected in nearly two decades. They live 50 to 125 meters deep and were caught by accident in nets. The A. aegis fish came up in 2006 near the Gambier Islands. Scientists could not dissect them, so micro-CT scans made 3D models of their skeletons. True seahorses have belly plates and a bony crown called a coronet; Australyichthys has neither. DNA from one preserved fish also placed it outside seahorses. Scientists call this look-alike pattern convergent evolution.
why_it_matters: It shows you that two creatures can look almost the same yet still be different, so checking small details matters when you compare things in everyday life.

background_read: A seahorse is a small fish with a horse-shaped head, a curled tail, and a pouch where males carry the young.
The helmethead sea muppet looks like a seahorse, but it has no belly plates and no bony crown, so scientists place it in a new group outside true seahorses.
When unrelated animals grow similar shapes, scientists call that convergent evolution.

WHY: DNA from one preserved fish and skeleton scans placed it outside seahorses, showing a look-alike pattern scientists call convergent evolution
